overview: This card follows the Lebanese Republic through the atlas's circa-1945-to-present display record. Lebanon ended the French mandate in 1943, the United States recognized it in 1944 and French forces left in 1946, so the map's opening year is a convenient layer date rather than a founding moment. Its repeated historical outlines and later modern polygon are approximate coverage, not a border-by-border account of wars or control.

periods.title: Independence completed and a new republic tested
periods.summary: French troops withdrew in 1946 after independence and recognition had already begun. The young republic also absorbed major regional and social pressures, including refugees after the 1948 war.

periods.title: Growth, a 1958 crisis and mounting strains
periods.summary: An armed political crisis erupted in 1958. Later prosperity coexisted with uneven development, confessional competition, Palestinian armed activity and pressures from neighboring conflicts.

periods.title: Civil war and foreign intervention
periods.summary: Civil war fractured the state among changing Lebanese and Palestinian forces while Syria and Israel intervened. Israel invaded in 1982; civilians endured siege, displacement and massacre.

periods.title: Taif institutions, reconstruction and Syrian influence
periods.summary: The Taif framework supported an end to open civil war and constitutional reform. Reconstruction followed while Syrian military and intelligence power remained deeply influential until 2005.

periods.title: Withdrawal, political shocks and uneasy continuity
periods.summary: Syrian forces withdrew in 2005, but the republic continued through assassinations, political deadlock, conflict and regional spillovers rather than entering a simple postwar calm.

periods.title: Financial collapse, explosions and renewed conflict
periods.summary: A financial crisis began in 2019, the 2020 Beirut port explosions devastated neighborhoods and later wars caused new damage and displacement. The World Bank's August 2026 outlook says March 2026 fighting interrupted a fragile 2025 recovery.

items.text: Lebanese leaders declared the French mandate ended in November 1943. US recognition followed in September 1944, diplomatic relations in November 1944 and the remaining French forces left in 1946. Those dates answer different questions: who claimed independence, who recognized it and when foreign soldiers withdrew. The atlas's 1945 start sits between them and should not be mistaken for the birthday of Lebanon.

Lebanon's constitution describes a parliamentary republic and protects religious communities' schools. Parliamentary seats are divided equally between Christians and Muslims, then proportionally among confessional groups and regions until a non-confessional electoral law is adopted. This arrangement was designed to share power in a diverse country, but a constitutional formula cannot by itself remove inequality, patronage or disagreement.

The republic's early decades mixed commerce and cultural life with serious fault lines. Refugees arrived after the 1948 Arab-Israeli war, and in 1958 armed conflict broke out among Lebanese factions amid wider regional rivalry. The crisis ended, but tensions over political representation, inequality and Palestinian armed organizations continued. By April 1975, one violent incident triggered a much larger breakdown that years of mistrust had prepared.

The civil war was not one two-sided contest. Alliances shifted among Lebanese militias and parties, Palestinian organizations and foreign states. Israel's 1982 invasion forced the PLO evacuation from Beirut. After Israeli forces entered West Beirut, Maronite militiamen massacred Palestinian civilians in Sabra and Shatila. Naming the perpetrators matters, and the crime must not be assigned to an entire religious community.

Lebanon's government sent the United Nations a July 1990 programme for implementing the Taif Charter. It called for constitutional reform, reconciliation, the restoration of state authority and the surrender of militia weapons. The programme helped move the country out of open civil war, but it was a plan to be carried out, not a magical switch. Institutions, neighborhoods and families still had to rebuild after fifteen years of violence.

Syrian forces and intelligence remained powerful in postwar Lebanon. A UN investigation records that Syrian forces withdrew in May 2005 after Security Council action, while also describing the earlier pervasive influence of Syrian military intelligence. Withdrawal changed the political landscape; it did not end domestic division, outside influence or armed conflict. A date on a troop movement is a milestone, not an instant cure.

Lebanon's financial crisis began in 2019, followed by the port explosions, pandemic pressures and wars. The World Bank estimated that the economy grew in 2025 after years of contraction, then projected a 6.4 percent contraction for 2026 after renewed fighting began in March. That August 2026 forecast is a dated snapshot. It shows how damaged housing, displacement, interrupted tourism and weakened banks reach ordinary household budgets.

sections.title: Archaeology, preservation and a very social breakfast

items.text: At Baalbek, enormous stone structures preserve layers of religious history. Phoenician traditions were joined to Hellenistic and Roman forms, and the Roman sanctuary rose over earlier remains. One terrace monolith weighs more than 800 tons, while columns of the Temple of Jupiter reached about 20 metres. These ancient feats belong to earlier societies; modern Lebanon's achievement is studying and caring for what survived.

UNESCO listed Baalbek in 1984. Lebanon's Directorate General of Antiquities has consolidated and restored monuments, while conservation plans try to protect the ruins from urban pressure and conflict damage. Archaeological discovery is not always a shiny object popping out of the ground; often it is patient comparison of walls, inscriptions and building layers, followed by the less glamorous superhero work of stopping stone from cracking.

After the 2020 port explosions, Li Beirut linked the repair of schools, museums, historic buildings and cultural livelihoods. By 2025, UNESCO reported training young heritage specialists, restoring major cultural sites and helping the Directorate General of Antiquities with storage and digitization equipment. Later teams also assessed conflict damage at Tyre and Baalbek. Preservation became both skilled employment and emergency response.

A familiar morning food is al-man'ouché: thin dough spread with mixtures that can include thyme, sumac, toasted sesame, salt and olive oil, then baked. People may add tomatoes, cucumbers, olives, mint, labneh or other cheeses and drink tea with it. It is breakfast with enough possible toppings to run a tiny election, although the most important vote may be whether anyone gets the last piece.

UNESCO describes parents teaching children how to prepare man'ouché and apprentices learning in small bakeries, many of them family-run. The morning trip to a neighborhood oven can become a social visit, and the food appears in homes and community gatherings across religious backgrounds. Daily life here is not just what people eat; it is who mixes the dough, who learns by watching and who chats while breakfast bakes.

The port explosions also brought a youth-led civic response. UNICEF and partners involved more than 1,900 young people in debris removal, small repairs, meal distribution and mask production; some had construction training through vocational courses. Their work did not erase the disaster or replace public responsibility. It does show teenagers and young adults turning practical skills into help for neighbors when streets, homes and services were damaged.

The constitution's Article 1 begins, “لبنان دولة مستقلة ذات وحدة لا تتجزأ وسيادة تامة”, officially rendered as “Lebanon is an independent, indivisible, and sovereign state.” Arabic is read from right to left, and Article 11 names it the national official language. This is a modern typed constitutional sample from an article amended in 1943, not an ancient inscription and not proof that every constitutional promise is always fulfilled.

Lebanon's constitution protects freedom of education and the right of religious communities to establish schools under general state rules. In practice, schooling has repeatedly been interrupted by financial crisis, displacement and fighting. A constitutional right supplies a legal foundation, while safe buildings, paid teachers, transport, electricity and family income determine whether a child can actually reach a desk and keep learning.

The 2020 port explosions damaged education across Beirut. UNESCO and partners completed rehabilitation of 280 educational institutions within eighteen months, including direct work on schools, vocational centres, university buildings and eleven school libraries. Reopening meant more than replacing windows: teams supplied furniture and equipment, restored libraries and trained teachers and librarians. A repaired classroom is infrastructure, but it is also a place where routines can return.

War damaged schools again in 2026. A September assessment by the Ministry of Education and UNICEF covered 1,089 facilities and found 436 damaged and 37 destroyed after hostilities that began in March. Education teams used in-person, distance and blended arrangements while planning repairs, learning recovery and psychosocial support. These figures are dated to that survey; they are not a permanent total in a changing emergency.

Beirut has trained physicians for generations. The medical school that became AUB's Faculty of Medicine opened in 1867, and its first doctors graduated in 1871. During the Second World War its bacteriology department produced vaccines used by local government. That is a chain from classroom to laboratory to public service, built long before the modern atlas layer and carried into the republic rather than invented overnight in 1945.

AUB's medical center kept treating casualties during the 1975-1990 civil war even as conflict damaged education and drove staff away. In a later era, Lebanon's Ministry of Public Health and WHO set 2026-2029 priorities that include primary care, hospitals, digital health, medicine management, workforce investment and emergency preparedness. Medical achievement includes discoveries and machines, but also keeping trained people and supplies working through a crisis.

sections.title: Water, toilets and the quiet machinery of daily life

items.text: Since the financial crisis began, many public water systems have struggled to power pumps, treat water and perform repairs. Some households have depended on costly private water trucks, while many wastewater plants have been non-functional or far below capacity. That means a kitchen tap and a toilet are connected to electricity, public finance and engineering. Plumbing may hide in the wall, but the systems behind it are enormous.

The same UNICEF programme records more than 500 repairs to water systems in 2024 and support for rehabilitating sixteen wastewater facilities by 2025. Repairs are a public-health achievement because treated water and safely handled sewage interrupt routes by which disease spreads. A wastewater plant will probably never win a beauty contest, but when it works, everyone downstream has a better day.

Displacement makes ordinary bathroom privacy much harder. During the 2024 emergency, UNICEF reports that work at 187 displacement sites installed 713 showers and 413 toilets. These were emergency facilities, not a measure of toilets in Lebanon as a whole. Still, the numbers reveal a basic truth children understand immediately: a shelter needs safe places to wash and go to the bathroom, not just mattresses and a roof.

After the Beirut port explosions, UNICEF and partners reported safe sanitation access for more than 197,000 people and public-water reconnections for more than 23,000. Other teams supplied hygiene kits, repaired schools and health facilities and supported families. A working toilet or water pipe may be less photogenic than a famous temple, yet it can decide whether a family can remain safely at home while a neighborhood recovers.

ending.text: Lebanon continues as a republic; this atlas record has no historical end date. Its 2100 geometry cutoff is a display horizon, not a forecast. As of September 2026, renewed conflict and damaged schools made continuity painfully practical: keeping government, family life, education, medicine, water and culture operating. Civil war, withdrawal, financial collapse and explosions changed institutions and daily routines, but none marks the disappearance of Lebanon or its people.
